reasons: The excerpt states that 13 of 135 tests won, that more tests lose than win, and that learnings from losing tests should be rolled into the next test.
It expressly says that someone must be able to understand why the test lost.
The case study explicitly concerns AOV plateauing between $60 and $80 and says the team set up full in-cart optimization.
The described implementation included shipping and gift thresholds that unlock with greater spend, in-cart upsells, and a reported nearly $60,000 monthly revenue increase.
The source reports "over 180,000 in monthly revenue increase" but does not attach a dollar sign or otherwise state the currency for that figure; the candidate changes it to "$180,000."

The described test also included a custom modal in which a customer could select a color for each item. That implementation step is omitted from the action despite being part of the source's account of the test.
The excerpt directly explains the result in the context of sunglasses costing approximately $30 to $40 rather than luxury-price products, and says customers are likely to own multiple pairs.

The source explicitly recommends transforming large product-description text blocks in GPT into benefit-driven bullet points, bolding key words, and emphasizing customer outcomes rather than features.
It conditions the recommendation on product pages that have big blocks of text.
The excerpt says the redesign was prompted by a need for greater clarity about the product, intended customer, and use case, along with stronger trust and engagement.

It explicitly describes testing a redesigned homepage hero with enhanced UX/UI and trust-building elements, including moved-up social proof, a clear headline, benefit bullets, product image, clear CTA, and trust seals.
The listed trust-seal examples—money-back guarantee, over 10,000 happy customers, vegan friendly, and made in the US—appear explicitly in the excerpt.
The source says the sales-page above-the-fold redesign introduced a trust policy bar, an outcome-driven higher-converting headline, benefit-driven bullet points, and one clear CTA.
It also expressly says the CTA should explain what happens after it is clicked and where the customer will go, and that post-purchase insights were used to find objections and friction.
The excerpt states, with similar uncertainty, that if the destination is unknown, something like "shop bestsellers" probably typically works best.
The excerpt explicitly says post-purchase insights were used to find common objections and friction points, including asking customers what almost stopped them from buying.
The source says most respondents identified uncertainty about leather quality as the near-purchase barrier and that the homepage had not articulated this friction point adequately.

It describes changing hero copy to address craftsmanship, leather quality and sourcing, handcrafted construction, and sandal quality, followed by a reported 77K monthly incremental increase. The source does not state the currency, and the candidate appropriately preserves it as "77K."

The source's stated request flow requires first scanning the QR code or visiting the provided URL, after which the person is redirected to the typeform. The candidate includes form completion but omits that required access step.
The offer is expressly qualified as having no obligation to use the agency and as something recipients can implement themselves; those material offer conditions are absent.
